stories.title_en: Luring Him to Drink and Whore, Ruining His Name

paragraphs.zh: 石涓，湖广麻城人。富而多诈，负气好胜，与族兄石涧尝争买田宅致隙。涧男石孝，读书进学，人品俊秀，性敏能文，人多拟其可中。石涓尝怀妒忌，思“吾生平发财，被涧兄所压。今其子又居士列，是虎而辅翼也。”因思计暗伤涧、孝父子。
paragraphs.en: Shi Juan was a native of Macheng in Huguang. Rich and full of deceit, he was touchy and hated to lose. He had once clashed with his elder cousin Shi Jian over rival bids for fields and houses, and bad blood remained between them. Jian's son Shi Xiao studied, won a place in the county school, and was handsome, quick-witted, and a gifted writer; many predicted he would pass the examinations. Shi Juan nursed his jealousy: "All my life I have made money, yet brother Jian has always held me down. Now his son has joined the ranks of the scholars—a tiger grown wings." So he cast about for a scheme to wound Jian and Xiao, father and son, in secret.

paragraphs.zh: 不数年，涧故。石孝居忧，无人检束。涓思孝年少不羁，或可诱以酒色。因伪相结纳，孝趋亦趋，孝诺亦诺，终日游戏相征逐，数以曲蘖为欢。或时有美妓，涓邀孝饮其邸；或有好戏妇，涓每搬戏邀孝饮，又令戏妇曲意奉承，务挑其淫荡之心。孝堕其术中而不觉，玩日月，荒废诗书。及服阕补考，竟列劣等。孝因发奋，往寺读书，涓辄拉友挟妓，载酒至寺欢饮。孝见妓，不觉有喜心，故态复萌。涓又劝孝娶美妾二人，朝夕纵淫。内荒于色，外湎于酒，手沾战疯，不能楷书。道考被黜，家业凋零。石涓抚掌大笑曰：“吾生平之恨泄矣，计亦遂矣！”乃呼其子而训之曰：“涧兄在日，家富于我。因生孝不肖，酷好饮酒宿娼，不事诗书，致令丧却前程，身如丧家之狗。尔辈宜以为鉴，慎勿踏其覆辙。”未几，其子亦被人引诱赌嫖，所费不訾。涓因年老，无如之何，唯付之长叹而已。
paragraphs.en: A few years later Jian died. Shi Xiao was in mourning, with no one to keep him in line. Juan thought: Xiao is young and unbridled; perhaps he can be baited with wine and women. So he feigned friendship and attached himself to the boy: where Xiao went, Juan went; whatever Xiao approved, Juan approved. They spent whole days chasing amusements together and made merry over wine again and again. Whenever a pretty courtesan appeared, Juan invited Xiao to drink at her house; whenever a good actress came to town, Juan would stage a play and invite Xiao to drink, telling the actress to fawn on him with every art, bent on stirring his lust. Xiao fell into the trap without knowing it. He idled away the months and let his books go to waste. When the mourning ended and he sat the make-up examination, he was placed in the bottom grade. Xiao then roused himself and went to study at a temple, but Juan would drag along friends and courtesans, carting wine to the temple for drinking bouts. At the sight of the courtesans Xiao's heart lifted despite himself, and his old habits sprouted again. Juan next urged Xiao to take two beautiful concubines, and he wallowed in lust morning and night. Wasted by sex within and soaked in wine without, his hands shook uncontrollably, and he could no longer write a steady hand. At the circuit examination he was struck off the rolls, and the family estate withered. Shi Juan clapped and roared with laughter: "The grudge of a lifetime is vented, and my scheme has succeeded!" Then he called his sons and lectured them: "While brother Jian lived, his house was richer than mine. But he sired that worthless Xiao, whose one love was drinking and whoring and who would not touch his books, so he threw away his future and ended up a homeless dog. Take him as a warning, and never follow in his ruts." Not long after, his own sons were led by others into gambling and whoring, and the money they burned through was beyond counting. Juan was old by then and could do nothing; he could only heave long sighs.

paragraphs.zh: 按：石涓奸巧百端，匿怨友人，使孝淫溺酒色，名利俱丧。彼虽自谓得计，足以快其宿忿，殊不思杀人之父，人亦杀其父；杀人之兄，人亦杀其兄。天网恢恢，报应不爽，安能保他人不袭彼故智，而子孙不蹈其覆辙乎？垂戒二子所繇，殆与义方之训异矣，又何怪其子之复然耶！然孝亦自愚也。使孝稍有心智，宜忖父在之时，与彼有怨，今父已即世，得彼不念足矣，顾安望深交乃尔！此其中情，叵测可知。由是以怠惰荒淫为戒，勤励不息自强，则石涓虽诈，安能中自立之士哉！
paragraphs.en: Note: Shi Juan employed a hundred crafty tricks. He concealed his grudge against a friend, feigned friendship with Xiao, and drowned him in wine and lust until he lost both his reputation and fortune. Though Juan thought he had won and could vent his long-held spite, he never considered that if one kills a man’s father, others will kill his father; if one kills a man’s brother, others will kill his brother. Heaven’s net is vast, and its retribution never fails. How could he be sure no one else would copy his old tricks, or that his own sons and grandsons would not follow the same path? The warning he gave his two sons was far removed from the teachings of a righteous father—so why be surprised that his sons turned out the same way? Yet Xiao was also foolish. Had he possessed even a shred of sense, he should have reasoned: while my father lived, this man was his enemy; now that my father has passed away, it would suffice if he let the grudge go—how could I expect such deep friendship? That something unfathomable lay behind this should have been clear. If Xiao had taken sloth and debauchery as a warning and driven himself on without rest, then however crafty Shi Juan was, how could he have deceived a man of independent spirit?

stories.title_en: Luring a Friend into Adultery to Scheme for His Land

paragraphs.zh: 毕和，山西人。心术狡险，阴悍暗毒，乡人无不被其害者。族弟毕松，有田一段，价值五十餘金，与和田毗连。和屡谋不遂，因诈与交好，屡席相款，旦夕游戏，即同胞不啻焉。
paragraphs.en: Bi He was a man of Shanxi. His mind was sly and vicious, secretly fierce and poisonous; there was hardly a villager he had not harmed. His clan younger brother Bi Song had a plot of land worth more than fifty taels, adjoining He’s fields. He had often schemed for it without success, so he pretended friendship, repeatedly treated Song to feasts, and amused himself with him morning and evening, no less close than full brothers.

paragraphs.zh: 同乡有林远者，性刚而暴。其妻罗氏，貌美好淫，与夫反睦〔目〕。和乘机挑之，遂通往来，情甚密。假意不令松知，实欲使之知之。故遮头露尾，为松觑破。松乃怪和曰：“枉自与你相知。有此美妇人，何不引我一宿，岂便夺你爱乎？”和逊谢曰：“此妇极有情，若引你去，必深相怜爱。恐你往来无节，事机不密，其夫若知，有误身家不便矣。”松只疑其专宠，乃私往挑之，罗氏遂允。后来情更绸缪，每候其夫出外，非和往则松往，甚且三人同床，情如一体。
paragraphs.en: In the same village lived a man named Lin Yuan, hard and violent by nature. His wife, Lady Luo, was beautiful and licentious, and she and her husband were at odds. He seized the opening and seduced her; they began an affair and grew very close. He pretended to keep it from Song while in fact wanting Song to find out—half hiding it, half letting it show—until Song saw through him. Song reproached him: "So much for our friendship. With a beauty like that, why not take me along for a night? Do you think I would steal her from you?" He answered with a show of deference: "The woman is full of feeling. If I brought you, she would surely dote on you. But I fear you would come and go without restraint, word would leak out, and if her husband found out, it could ruin your household and endanger your life." Song only suspected He of keeping her all to himself, so he went on his own to seduce her, and Luo gave in. After that the affair grew still more tangled: whenever the husband was out, if it was not He who went, it was Song; at times all three even shared one bed, close as a single body.

paragraphs.zh: 将及月餘，和密报其夫曰：“松弟与我至知，今闻与令正有情，我屡谏不听。闻你欲捕之，若捕得，可轻打些。彼必叫我解交，我谕他多送你些银，以绝他后日妄为。慎勿害他性命。”林远闻言，怒气填胸。次日即托言外出，须三日后方归。松专瞰远去向，闻其出外，即往其家，搂罗氏入房调耍。林远从密处突出，打入房中，二人已解衣在床。远揪松于床下凶打，罗氏拼命拿住夫手，远不能多打。松求放曰：“愿以银赎免。”远曰：“要何人来保认？”松曰：“叫我和兄来。”远正合意，即遣人呼和至。和曰：“不行正路，以至于此。须召见你亲兄来。”松曰：“勿召我兄，只你代我出银与之，后日即还。”和曰：“我代议事，怎好出银？但今事急矣，我若不出银，此事无由解释。然必有实物相当方可。”松因写前毗连之田契卖之。和曰：“只可少作价，多则亦为林远所得。”止作价四十两。和归，取银三十两相付。远曰：“须六十两。”和曰：“奸情被获，合输妇价一半。纵令正美貌，可值六十金，此已一半矣。”远再三不肯。和曰：“彼田价四十两，我手中无现银，不如约一月后，再在我手接十两。”远要约批。和曰：“若他人议事，须加二抽头，我已该八两矣。今为你息事，何逼我约批乎？”遂无约批，放松同归。
paragraphs.en: When nearly a month had passed, He secretly tipped off the husband: “Song is my dearest friend, but now I hear he is carrying on with your wife. I have warned him again and again and he will not listen. I hear you mean to catch them. If you do, give him only a light beating. He is sure to call me in to mediate, and I will make him pay you a good sum of silver to put an end to his mischief. Whatever you do, do not take his life.” Lin Yuan heard this and rage filled his chest. The next day he announced he was going out and would not be back for three days. Song had been watching for Yuan’s departure; the moment he heard the man was away, he went to the house, pulled Luo into the bedroom, and began to fool around. Lin Yuan burst out of hiding and charged into the room, where the two had already undressed on the bed. Yuan hauled Song off the bed and beat him savagely; Luo threw herself on her husband’s arms with all her strength, so Yuan could not land many blows. Song begged for release: “Let me buy my way out with silver.” Yuan said: “Who will stand surety for you?” Song said: “Fetch my sworn brother He.” That was exactly what Yuan wanted, and he sent for He at once. He said: “You strayed from the straight path, and it has come to this. We must call your own elder brother.” Song said: “Don’t call my brother. Just put up the silver for me and I will pay you back in a few days.” He said: “I came to mediate—how can I be the one paying? But the matter is urgent. If I do not put up the silver, there is no way out of this. Still, there must be real property to match it.” So Song wrote out a deed selling He the adjoining field. He said: “You can only price it low; any more would just end up in Lin Yuan’s pocket.” They set the price at a mere forty taels. He went home, brought back thirty taels, and handed them over. Yuan said: “I want sixty.” He said: “For adultery caught in the act, the forfeit is half the wife’s value. Even granting your wife is a beauty worth sixty taels, this is already half.” Yuan refused again and again. He said: “His field is priced at forty taels, and I have no more ready silver on hand. Better to agree that a month from now he collects another ten taels from me.” Yuan demanded a written receipt. He said: “If anyone else had mediated, he would take a twenty percent cut—I would already be owed eight taels. Here I am settling your affair for nothing, and you press me for a note?” So no note was written, and He took Song home with him.

paragraphs.zh: 数日后，松备本息四十四两赎前田，和不肯退。一月后，林远向和取约银。和曰：“指示你撰银三十两，二两谢我，岂为多乎？”远后对人说出和教捉奸之由，松方知为和所卖。然已堕其诡计，悔无及矣。
paragraphs.en: A few days later Song brought principal and interest—forty-four taels—to redeem the field, but He refused to return it. A month later Lin Yuan came to He for the promised silver. He said: "I showed you how to swindle thirty taels; is two taels in thanks too much to ask?" Yuan later told others how He had instigated him to catch the adulterers, and only then did Song learn that He had sold him out. But he had already fallen into the trap, and regret came too late.

paragraphs.zh: 按：和欲谋松田，先引之奸；欲诱其奸，先与之友。且其奸也，非彼明引，而令其自入。其要之田也，俟其有急而为之解纷，以徐收之，计亦巧矣。向非赖后约银，则林远必不言其所由，彼和之深情厚毒，畴能测之？故人而毒行不端者，彼虽与我交密，亦须提防者也。
paragraphs.en: Note: To get Song’s field, he first led him into adultery; to lure him into adultery, he first made himself Song’s friend. Nor did he openly push Song into the affair—he let Song walk into it on his own. As for claiming the field, he waited until Song was in desperate straits, then ‘settled the quarrel’ for him and quietly took possession. A clever scheme indeed. Had it not been for the silver promised afterward, Lin Yuan would never have revealed how it began, and who could have fathomed the depth of He’s feigned affection and his hidden venom? Thus, when a man’s conduct is venomous and crooked, even if he is close to you, you must keep your guard up.

stories.title_en: Scheming with a Friend's Wealth to Ruin His House

paragraphs.zh: 金从宇、洪起予，俱是应天府人。相隔一十餘店，皆开大京铺，各有资本千餘金。但从宇狡猾奸险，起予温良朴实。时常贩买京货，累相会席，各有酒量，欢相劝酬。
paragraphs.en: Jin Congyu and Hong Qiyu were both men of Yingtian Prefecture. Their shops stood a dozen or so doors apart, and both ran large stores dealing in goods from the capital, each with capital of more than a thousand taels. But Congyu was sly and deceitful, while Qiyu was gentle, honest, and simple. Both often traveled to buy Beijing merchandise and frequently met for banquets; each could hold his wine, and they toasted one another merrily.

paragraphs.zh: 从宇思曰：“人言慈不掌兵，义不掌财。我观起予慈善好义，诚直无智。何彼铺买卖与我相并也？当以智术笼络之。”以故伪相交密，时节以物相馈送，有庆贺礼，皆相请召。起予只以金为好意，皆薄来厚往以答之。从宇曰：“此人好酒，须以酒误之。”乃时时饮月福、打平和、邀庆纲，招饮殆无虚日。有芳辰佳景，邀与同游；夜月清凉，私谈竟夕。起予果中其奸，日在醉乡，不事买卖。从宇虽日伴起予游饮，彼有弟济宇在店，凡事皆能代理。起予一向闲游，店中虚无人守。有客来店者，寻之不在，多往济宇铺买。由是金铺日盛，洪铺日替，起予渐穷于用。从宇随取随与之，每一半九成，一半七八成；银又等头轻少，不索其借批，但云“须明白记帐也”。不四五年间，陆续借上六百餘两。乃使济宇往取之，起予别借二百两以还。后算过帐，尚欠四百餘两。逼其写田宅为当，方思还债取田。起予一皆从言。再过两年，本息合四百五十餘两矣。济宇力逼全收。起予求从宇稍宽。从宇曰：“吾银本与舍弟相共，彼在家尝怨我不合把银借你。今我不理，任你两下何如？”此时金宅有新立当契在手，起予推延不过，只得将产业尽数写契填还之。他债主知其落寞，都来逼取。千餘金家，不两三栽，一旦罄空。皆金从宇倾陷累算之故也。
paragraphs.en: Congyu thought: “As the saying goes, the kind cannot command troops and the upright cannot hold on to money. I see that Qiyu is charitable and fond of doing good, honest and without guile. Why should his shop’s trade rival mine? I must snare him with craft.” So he feigned close friendship: he sent gifts at every season, and whenever there was a celebration he invited Qiyu. Qiyu took Jin’s attentions as goodwill and always returned small gifts with generous ones. Congyu said: “The man loves wine; wine will be his ruin.” So he kept up a round of monthly banquets, split-the-bill dinners, and guild celebrations—there was hardly a day without a drinking invitation. On fine days with lovely views he took Qiyu roaming; on cool moonlit nights they talked in private until dawn. Qiyu duly fell for the trap: he spent his days in a drunken haze and gave no thought to business. Congyu might spend his days drinking and roaming with Qiyu, but he had a younger brother, Jiyu, in the shop who could manage everything. Qiyu idled away his time while his own shop stood empty and unwatched. Customers who came looking for him and found him gone mostly went to buy at Jiyu’s shop instead. So Jin’s shop flourished by the day while Hong’s declined by the day, and Qiyu gradually ran short of funds. Congyu gave him money whenever he asked—but each time half of it was ninety-percent silver and half only seventy or eighty, and the weight came up light on the scale. He never asked for a loan note, only saying, “Just keep a clear account.” In less than four or five years the loans had mounted to more than six hundred taels. Then he sent Jiyu to collect. Qiyu borrowed two hundred taels elsewhere to repay, and when the accounts were settled he still owed more than four hundred. They pressed him to sign over his fields and houses as a mortgage—Qiyu meaning to repay the debt later and redeem the land. Qiyu went along with everything they said. Two more years passed, and principal and interest together came to more than four hundred fifty taels. Jiyu pressed hard to collect in full. Qiyu begged Congyu for a little leniency. Congyu said: “My silver is held in common with my younger brother. At home he has often complained that I should never have lent it to you. I will stay out of it now—settle it between the two of you.” By then the Jin household held the freshly written mortgage deed. Qiyu could stall no longer and had to sign over every property he owned to cover the debt. His other creditors, seeing him ruined, all came pressing for payment. A household worth more than a thousand taels was emptied in a stroke within two or three years. It was all the work of Jin Congyu’s entrapment and compounded scheming.

paragraphs.zh: 洪已破家之后，从宇全不瞅睐，虽求分文相借，一毫不与矣。从宇又用此术，再交杨店之子。有识者笑杨子曰：“汝是洪起予替身，何不取鉴前车乎？”杨乃渐疏绝之。
paragraphs.en: Once Hong’s house was broken, Congyu would not spare him a glance; even if he begged to borrow a single cash, not a hair was given. Congyu then applied the same art to the son of the Yang shop. Those who saw through it laughed at young Yang: “You are Hong Qiyu’s replacement—why not learn from the cart that overturned ahead of you?” Yang gradually drew away and cut him off.

paragraphs.zh: 按：以银借人，收其子利，未为累算。特洪本富贾，从宇诱其游饮，不事生理，致资本消折，而以银借之。期间以八当十，加三算息，亏短田价，稍蚕食之。从宇之奸贪极矣！为富不仁，从宇其何说之辞？
paragraphs.en: Note: Lending silver to others and taking interest is not, by itself, compounding a trap. The point is that Hong was originally a rich merchant, and Congyu lured him into roaming and drinking so he neglected his livelihood, his capital shrank, and then he lent him silver. In between he counted eight as ten, charged thirty percent interest, shorted the land price, and slowly ate him like a silkworm. Congyu’s greed and treachery reached the extreme! The rich who are not humane—what excuse can Congyu offer?

stories.title_en: Goading a Friend into an Adultery Suit to Ruin His House

paragraphs.zh: 马自鸣，浙江绍兴人。狷巧小人，柔媚多奸。族弟马应，轻浮愚昧，家更富于自鸣。其父素与鸣父不睦，两相图而未发。自鸣见应愚呆，性又嗜酒，故时时与之会饮；亦连引诸人，共打平和。唯此两人深相结纳，人多厌之，不与共饮。二人乃对斟对酌，此唱彼和，自号为莫逆交。应有事，多取决于自鸣；鸣亦时献小计，以效忠款。应素与亲兄不睦，数扬其短，欲状告之。自鸣假意劝阻，实于当机处反言以激之，益深其怒。应遂先往告兄，经官断明，拟应欧兄之罪；又投分上解释。此为破家之始。又屡屡唆其与人争讼，家日破败。
paragraphs.en: Ma Ziming was a native of Shaoxing in Zhejiang—a small-minded schemer, smooth and fawning and full of guile. His younger cousin Ma Ying was flighty and dull, and his household was even richer than Ziming's. Ying's father had long been at odds with Ziming's father; each side was plotting against the other, but neither had struck. Ziming saw that Ying was a fool and a drunk besides, so he drank with him constantly, sometimes rounding up others to share the cost. But only these two formed a real bond; everyone else grew sick of them and would not drink with them. So the two poured for each other, sang each other's praises, and called themselves bosom friends. Whenever Ying had business, he mostly let Ziming decide, and Ziming would offer little schemes from time to time to prove his devotion. Ying had long been on bad terms with his own elder brother; he often aired the man's faults and wanted to file a complaint against him. Ziming made a show of talking him out of it, but at the decisive moment he would say just the opposite to provoke him, and Ying's anger deepened. Ying went ahead and accused his brother first. The officials saw the case clearly and found Ying guilty of assaulting an elder brother; he got off only by calling in favors. This was the beginning of the family's ruin. After that Ziming egged him into lawsuit after lawsuit, and the household crumbled by the day.

paragraphs.zh: 后自鸣往小户人家取债，见其妇幼美，归家向应前夸曰：“我今往某家取债，其媳妇生甚美貌，女流中西施也。我以目挑之，俯首而过。其屋只一楹，数往来于前。我神魂飘荡，不能自禁。又以笑语挑之，此妇亦笑脸回答，似亦可图。只怕其夫姑有碍，未敢施为。至今挂恋在心，寤寐思服。”应曰：“此家是我甲首，又系佃户，图亦何难？我必先取之。”自鸣激之曰：“汝若能得，我输你一大东道。依我说，勿去惹此愚夫，若捉住，彼粗拳，真打死也。”应曰：“未闻佃客敢殴主人者。”次日，即往其家收条编。一见其妇，即挑之，遣其婆出外曰：“可外出觅菜来作午。”婆方出，即强抱其妇入房。妇在从否之间，见隔壁一妇窥见躲开。妇指之曰：“某姆在隔壁窥见，你勿为此。”哪肯休，只以为推托也。相缠已久，婆在外归。妇只得叫妈妈曰：“主人如此野意。”婆作色叱。怒，先往县呈其拖欠条编，反允殴里长。其佃人以强奸诉官拘审，邻妇窥见，亲姑捉获。其妇又貌美倾城，满堂聚观，啧啧叹赏。因审作强奸，应拟死罪。后投分上，改作戏奸未就。而家业尽倾，田宅皆卖与自鸣。（自鸣）反责曰：“我当初叫你勿为，你不听吾言，以至于此。”应曰：“你口虽叫我勿为，先已造桥，送我在桥中去矣，难回步也。今欲怪你，又怪不得。孟子谓‘非之无可举，刺之无可刺’，正你这样人也。”
paragraphs.en: Later Ziming went to a humble household to collect a debt and saw that the wife was young and beautiful. He came home and boasted to Ying: “Today I went to such-and-such a house to collect a debt. The daughter-in-law is a rare beauty, a veritable Xi Shi among women. I made eyes at her and she passed with her head bowed. The house is only one bay wide, so I strolled back and forth in front of it several times. My soul went adrift and I could not help myself. Then I teased her with laughing words, and she answered with a smile—she seemed there for the taking. My only fear was that her husband and his mother would be in the way, so I dared not act. I have been pining for her ever since, waking and sleeping.” Ying said: “That household is one of my tithing heads (jiashou), and they are my tenants besides. What is hard about having her? I will take her first.” Ziming provoked him: “If you can have her, I will stand you a grand feast. But take my advice: do not provoke that dolt of a husband. If he catches you, those coarse fists of his will beat you to death for real.” Ying said: “I have never heard of a tenant daring to lay a hand on his landlord.” The next day he went to the house to collect the consolidated tax. The moment he saw the wife he began teasing her, and sent her mother-in-law out: “Go find some vegetables for lunch.” As soon as the old woman left, he seized the wife and dragged her into the bedroom. She wavered between yielding and refusing; then she saw a woman next door peek in and duck away. She pointed: “Auntie next door saw us—you mustn’t.” He would not stop, taking it for a mere excuse. They had been grappling for a good while when the old woman came back. The wife could only cry out, “Mother! The master is forcing himself on me!” The old woman flared up and scolded him. Enraged, Ying went straight to the county and filed a complaint that the household had defaulted on the consolidated tax, and even accused them of assaulting the village head (lizhang). The tenant in turn accused Ying of rape, and the officials arrested the parties for trial. The neighbor woman had seen it, and the wife’s own mother-in-law had caught them. The wife was, moreover, a stunning beauty; the whole courtroom crowded in to stare, clucking in admiration. The case was tried as rape, and Ying was sentenced to death. Later he called in favors and had the charge reduced to attempted seduction, not consummated. But the family estate was ruined; the fields and houses were all sold to Ziming. And Ziming had the gall to scold him: “I told you at the start not to do it. You would not listen, and it has come to this.” Ying said: “Your mouth told me not to, but you had already laid a trap that left me no way back—I walked right into it. I want to blame you, yet I cannot quite pin it on you. Mencius said, ‘Condemn him and there is nothing to cite; censure him and there is nothing to seize.’ That is exactly a man like you.”

paragraphs.zh: 田卖尽，自鸣绝不与往来。朝夕相借，惟干谒亲兄，方知亲者终是亲；彼酒肉朋友，真伪情也。
paragraphs.en: Once all the land was sold, Ziming cut off all dealings with him. Borrowing morning and night, Ying found that only his own elder brother would help him. Only then did he realize that blood is blood after all, and that those wine-and-meat friends were false from the start.

paragraphs.zh: 按：应被自鸣笼络，家破，产业尽被鸣收之，反与之莫逆之交，何其愚也！苟有心智人之处世，内而兄弟叔侄，外而朋友亲戚，皆不能无。与兄结讼而求昵于友，是其所厚者薄，而薄者反厚也。何不观孙荣之间革孙华而亦昵于友，使非杨氏贤德，后始有悔悟。而能以是而自新之，彼虽有百般巧计，安能中自新之士哉！
paragraphs.en: Note: Ying was ensnared by Ziming; his household was ruined and all his property seized by Ziming, yet he treated him as an unbreakable friend. How foolish! Any sensible person navigating life cannot do without brothers, uncles, and nephews within the family, nor without friends and kin beyond it. To sue one's own brother while seeking intimacy with a friend is to slight those one should cherish and cherish those one should slight. Consider Sun Rong, who drove out his brother Sun Hua and clung to his friends instead: had his wife Lady Yang not been virtuous, he would have repented too late. But if a man can truly renew himself, then however many clever tricks they devise, how could they possibly succeed against such a renewed soul?

stories.title_en: A Cunning Broker Cheats on the Paper and Repays with His Daughter

paragraphs.zh: 施守训，福建大安人。家资殷富，常造纸卖客。一日，自装千餘篓，价值八百餘两，往苏州卖，寓牙人翁滨二店。滨乃宿牙，叠积前客债甚多，见施雏商，将其纸尽还前客，误施坐候半年。家中又发纸五百餘篓到苏州，滨代现卖。付银讫，托言系取旧帐者，复候半年。知受其笼络，施乃怒骂殴之。滨无言可应，当凭乡亲刘光前议，谕滨立过借批银八百两，劝施暂回。
paragraphs.en: Shi Shouxun was a native of Da'an in Fujian. His family was wealthy, and he regularly made paper to sell to merchants. One day he loaded more than a thousand baskets himself, worth over eight hundred taels, and went to Suzhou to sell them, lodging at the shop of the broker Weng Bin'er. Weng was an old hand among brokers and had piled up heavy debts to earlier clients. Seeing that Shi was a novice merchant, he used the entire shipment of paper to pay off those earlier clients, leaving Shi waiting for half a year. Shi's family then sent another five hundred-odd baskets of paper to Suzhou, and Weng sold them for him for cash. When the silver came in, he claimed it had gone to settle old accounts, and Shi waited another half a year. Realizing he had been strung along, Shi cursed him and beat him. Weng had no answer. With their fellow townsman Liu Guangqian mediating, Weng was made to write out an IOU for eight hundred taels, and Shi was advised to head home for the time being.

paragraphs.zh: 次年，复载纸到苏州，滨代现卖。只前帐难还，施又坐待半年。见其女云英有貌，未曾许配，思此银难取，乃浼刘光前为媒，求其女为妾，抵还前帐。滨悦许之。其女年方十五，执不肯从。滨与妻入劝曰：“古有缇萦愿没官为婢，以赎父罪。今父欠客人银八百两，以汝填还；况福建客家多巨富，若后日生子，分其家财，居此致富，享福非小。”女始允诺。时施已六十餘矣。成婚近四载，施后回家身故。未及周期服，滨将女重嫁南京溧水县梁恩赐为妾，重收聘礼一百两。
paragraphs.en: The next year Shi again shipped paper to Suzhou, and Weng sold it for cash. But the old debt remained hard to recover, so Shi waited in vain for another half-year. He noticed that Weng's daughter Yunying was good-looking and not yet betrothed. Thinking the silver would be difficult to collect, he asked Liu Guangqian to act as matchmaker and sought the daughter as a concubine to offset the debt. Weng happily agreed. The girl had just turned fifteen and flatly refused. Weng and his wife went in to press her: "In ancient times the girl Tiying offered to become a state slave to ransom her father from punishment. Now your father owes a client eight hundred taels of silver, and we are making it good with you. Besides, Fujian merchant families are often immensely rich; if you later bear a son and get a share of the family property, you will be set up in wealth here and enjoy no small fortune." Only then did the girl consent. Shi was already over sixty. They were married nearly four years; later Shi returned home and died. Before the mourning year was out, Weng remarried the girl as a concubine to Liang Enci of Lishui County, Nanjing, and collected another hundred taels in betrothal gifts.

paragraphs.zh: 守训男施钦知之为，本年亦装纸到苏州，往拜翁家，呼翁为“外祖”。翁不瞅睬他。请庶母出见，亦拒不出。众客伙皆怒而嗾曰：“你父以八百两聘礼，止成亲四载，未期服又重嫁他人。今一出见何害？情甚可恶！汝何不鸣官？”钦乃告于巡街蔡御史。时翁滨二得施为婿，复振家风，又发资金千餘，见告，毫无惧意。两下各投分上，讦讼几二年。各司道皆纳分上，附会而判。后钦状告刑部，始获公断曰：“翁滨二以女抵偿八百两，几与绿珠同价矣。但守训自肯，其财礼勿论。今夫服未满重嫁梁客，兜重财物，是以女为货，不顾律法。合责三十板，断身资银一百两，并守训为云英置衣资首饰银五十两，共与施钦领之。”因此积讼连年，滨二之家财尽倾，仍流落于贫矣。
paragraphs.en: When Shouxun's son Shi Qin learned of this, that same year he too shipped paper to Suzhou. He went to pay his respects at the Weng house and addressed Weng as "maternal grandfather." Weng ignored him. He asked for his stepmother to come out and see her; she too refused to come out. The other merchants there were angry and egged him on: "Your father paid eight hundred taels in betrothal gifts, they were man and wife only four years, and before the mourning period was over she was married off to another man. What harm would it do her to come out and see you once? The whole thing is outrageous! Why don't you report it to the authorities?" Qin then filed a complaint with the street-patrol censor Cai. By then Weng Bin'er, having gained Shi as a son-in-law, had restored the family fortunes and invested another thousand-plus taels in capital, so when the complaint came he felt not the slightest fear. Both sides enlisted backers, and the litigation dragged on nearly two years. Every office that handled the case took bribes and twisted the facts to decide it. Only when Qin filed with the Ministry of Justice did he get a fair judgment: "Weng Bin'er paid off eight hundred taels with his daughter — nearly the price of Lüzhu, the most costly concubine of old. But since Shouxun consented of his own accord, we will not go into the betrothal money. Now, before her husband's mourning period was complete, she was married off again to the merchant Liang, scooping up a second payment — this is treating a daughter as merchandise, with no regard for the law. He shall be beaten thirty strokes, and we award the body-price of one hundred taels, plus the fifty taels Shouxun spent on clothes and jewelry for Yunying, all to be paid over to Shi Qin." Because the lawsuits piled up year after year, Bin'er's family wealth was entirely drained, and he sank back into poverty.

paragraphs.zh: 按：脱骗之害，首侠棍，次狡侩。侠棍设局暗脱，窃盗也。狡侩骗货明卖，强盗也。二者当与盗同科。凡牙侩之弊，客货入店，彼皆作纲抵偿，又多窃取供家，每以后客货盖前客帐，此穷牙常态也。施守训在不早审牙家，致落此坑堑。只可小心逼取，或继以告，不当图其女为妾。夫以六旬上人，岁月几何，纳妾异地，能无后患乎？贻子后讼，所费不资。虽最终取胜，得不偿失矣。独恨翁滨二负心歹汉，以一女而还银八百两，得已过分，又得婿扶以成家；后女虽再嫁，当以身资还施之男，永可无患矣。乃贪心不满，再致倾家，真可为欺心负义之鉴。
paragraphs.en: Note: Of the harm done by swindles, the worst offenders are the bold rogues, and next the cunning brokers. The bold rogues set up schemes to cheat you in the dark—that is theft. The cunning brokers cheat you out of your goods and sell them openly—that is robbery. Both should be punished as bandits. As for the usual abuses of brokers: once a client's goods come into the shop, they lump them in to cover their debts, and they often skim off more for their own households; they habitually use a later client's goods to cover an earlier client's account. This is the normal state of a poor broker. Shi Shouxun's mistake was not sizing up the broker early on, so he fell into this pit. He should have pressed carefully for payment, or followed up with a lawsuit; he should not have schemed to take the daughter as a concubine. A man past sixty—how many years could he have left? Taking a concubine in a strange place—how could there not be trouble afterward? He left his son a lawsuit, and the costs were beyond counting. Though he won in the end, the gain did not cover the loss. What is hateful is Weng Bin'er, a heartless scoundrel: with one daughter he repaid eight hundred taels, already more than enough, and on top of that got a son-in-law's help to rebuild his household. Later, even when the girl remarried, he should have returned the body-price to Shi's son, and there would have been no trouble ever after. But his greedy heart was not satisfied, and he brought ruin on his house a second time. Truly this can serve as a warning mirror for those who cheat their conscience and betray what is right.

stories.title_en: A Poor Broker Gets Away with the Wax to Pay Old Debts

paragraphs.zh: 张霸，四川人。为人机关精密，身长力勇。一日，买蜡百餘担，往福建建宁府丘店发卖。此牙家盆彻骨，外张富态，欠前客货银极多。霸蜡到，即以光棍顶作鬼名来借蜡，约后还银。数日后，霸往街游玩，其蜡遍在诸铺。及问其姓名，皆与帐名不同。霸心疑必有弊，故回店讯问牙人曰：“你脱我蜡去还前帐，可一一实报帐来。若不实言，你乘我几拳不得。”丘牙哑口无应。霸轮拳擒打，如鹰擒雀，如踢戏球。丘牙连忙求饶，曰：“公神人也。此蜡真还前客旧帐，并家用去矣，何能问各店重取？”张霸曰：“你将还人的及各店买去的，都登上帐，只说他揭借去，俱未还银。我将帐去告，取你硬作证，怕他各店不再还我？”丘牙依言，一一写成发货帐。
paragraphs.en: Zhang Ba was a native of Sichuan, shrewd and meticulous in his schemes, tall and strong. One day he bought over a hundred loads of wax and went to sell it at Qiu's shop in Jianning Prefecture, Fujian. This broker was stingy to the bone yet put on a wealthy appearance, owing vast sums of silver to previous clients. When Ba's wax arrived, the broker sent sharpers under false names to borrow the wax, promising to pay the silver later. A few days later, Ba strolled through the streets and found his wax spread across all the shops. When he asked for the buyers' names, none matched those on the account. Suspecting foul play, he returned to the shop and questioned the broker: "You have made off with my wax to settle old debts. Report every account truthfully. If you do not speak plainly, you will not escape a few punches." Broker Qiu fell silent. Ba swung his fists, pummeling him like a hawk seizing a sparrow, like kicking a ball about. Qiu hastily begged for mercy: "Sir, you are a god! That wax truly went to pay earlier clients' old accounts and for household use; how could I ask the shops to return it?" Zhang Ba said: "Write down what you repaid to people and what the shops bought, recording only that they borrowed it on credit and have not yet paid the silver. I will take this ledger to file a complaint, using you as my witness. Why should I fear the shops won't pay me again?" Qiu did as told and wrote out the delivery ledger item by item.

paragraphs.zh: 张霸即具状告府。署印梅爷看状，掷地不准。霸心伤失本，两眼自然垂。再三哀告，梅爷乃准其状。先差皂隶往查各店蜡。霸以银贿公差，回报曰：“各店果有张霸印号蜡。”梅爷曰：“哪有揭借客蜡都不还银者！”即出牌拘审。
paragraphs.en: Zhang Ba then drew up a complaint and filed it with the prefecture. The acting prefect, Master Mei, read the complaint, threw it on the ground, and refused to accept it. Ba was heartsick at losing his capital and looked utterly crestfallen. After he pleaded again and again, Master Mei accepted the complaint. He first sent yamen runners to check the wax in the shops. Ba bribed the runners with silver, and they reported back: "The shops do indeed have wax bearing Zhang Ba's stamp." Master Mei said: "Who ever heard of taking a client's wax on credit and never paying the silver!" He at once issued a warrant to bring them in for trial.

paragraphs.zh: 各店在外商量曰：“我店买张客蜡，俱已还银，牙家收讫。又牙人自用蜡还我者，是他所合抽得牙钱，何得今更重告？吾与汝等敛银共用，投一分上，先去讲明，然后对审。”敛银已毕，即将银一百两投梅爷乡亲。
paragraphs.en: The shops conferred among themselves outside: "Our shops bought merchant Zhang's wax and have already paid the silver; the broker received it. And the wax the broker used to repay us on his own account was the brokerage cut he was entitled to take. How can he now sue us over it a second time? Let us pool silver for the expenses, submit a portion as a bribe, explain our side first, and then face the trial." When the silver had been collected, they sent one hundred taels to a fellow townsman of Master Mei.

paragraphs.zh: 梅爷刚正之官，弗听，即拘来审。内有江店客人，乃惯讼者，先对理曰：“蜡乃丘牙明卖与我，公平交易，张霸安得重取？即未全交付，亦牙家刻落，与我辈何干？”丘牙曰：“蜡非卖他。是小人先欠诸店旧帐，张霸蜡到，他等诈言措借，数日后即还银。及得蜡到手，即坐以抵前帐。非小人敢兜客银也。”梅爷曰：“丘牙欠债，须问彼自取，安得坐客人货以还彼债？你众等可将价还张霸，免你等罪。”江店恃有分上，再三辩论，说是明白交易，并无对债之事。梅爷触怒，将江店责十板；江店又辩论不已，又被责二十板。后诸人惊惧，皆称愿赔求饶。以江店监禁，诸人讨保，断蜡银，限三日，不完再重责。三日果追完。霸领银讫，深感梅爷恩泽，顶戴香炉，到于堂下，叩拜而去。
paragraphs.en: Master Mei, an upright official, would not listen to their pleas and ordered them brought in for trial. Among them was the man from the Jiang shop, a habitual litigant, who argued first: 'The wax was sold openly by Qiu the broker—a fair transaction. How can Zhang Ba demand payment again? Even if it wasn't fully paid, that is the broker's deduction—what does it have to do with us?' Qiu the broker replied: "The wax was not sold to them. I already owed old debts to the shops. When Zhang Ba's wax arrived, they falsely claimed they would borrow it and pay silver within a few days. Once they got the wax, they held onto it to offset the old debts. It is not that I dared to pocket the client's silver." Master Mei said: "If Qiu the broker owes debts, you must collect from him directly. How can you hold a client's goods to repay his debts? All of you will pay the price to Zhang Ba, and I will spare you punishment." The Jiang shop man, relying on his connections, argued repeatedly that it was a straightforward transaction with no debt offsetting. Master Mei grew angry and ordered him beaten ten strokes; when the man still refused to stop arguing, he was beaten twenty more. Then the others, terrified, all declared willingness to pay and begged for mercy. The Jiang man was imprisoned, while the rest secured guarantors. The wax money was assessed with a three-day deadline; if unpaid, they would be beaten again. Indeed, within three days, the full amount was collected. Ba received the silver and, deeply grateful for Master Mei's kindness, came before the hall carrying an incense burner in honor, kowtowed, and departed.

paragraphs.zh: 按：出外为商，以缥缈之身，涉寡亲之境，全仗经纪以为耳目。若遇经纪公正，则货物有主；一投狡侩，而抑货亏价必矣。是择经纪，乃经商一大关系也，可不慎哉！如其人言谈直率，此是公正之人。若初会晤间，上下估看，方露微言，则其心中狡猾可知。若价即言而不远，应对迟慢，心必怀欺。若屋宇精致，分外巧样，多是奢华务外之人，内必不能积聚。倘衣补垢腻，人鄙形猥，肩耸目光，巾帽不称寒暑，此皆贫穷之辈。若巧异妆扮，服色变常，必非创置之人，其内必无财钞。若衣冠不华，惟服布衣，此乃老实本分，不可以斯之曰贫。商而知此，何至如张霸，被牙所脱也？况非刚正之梅爷，肯听分上，几乎素手归矣。故录之，以示为商者。当货物发脱之初，细审经纪对手，发落方可保无虞矣。
paragraphs.en: Note: When you go abroad to trade, a lone drifter in a land of few kin, you rely entirely on the broker as your eyes and ears. If you meet an honest broker, your goods have a master; once you fall in with a cunning one, your goods will be held back and your price cheated — that is certain. So choosing a broker is one of the great matters of trade; how can you not be careful? If a man's talk is straight and frank, he is an honest man. If at the first meeting he sizes you up and down and only then lets slip a few words, you can tell his mind is sly. If he names a price readily and it is not far off the mark, yet his replies are slow and halting, his heart must harbor deceit. If his house is finely built and fancier than it needs to be, he is usually a showy, extravagant man who cannot have saved much inside. If his clothes are patched and greasy, his look mean and his frame shabby, his shoulders hunched and his gaze shifty, his cap and kerchief out of season — these are all poor men. If he dresses in clever, outlandish ways and his colors are out of the ordinary, he is surely not a man who has built anything up, and he has no cash inside. If his cap and gown are plain and he wears only cloth, that is an honest, steady man; you cannot call him poor on that account. If a merchant knows this, how would he end up like Zhang Ba, having been made off with by a broker? And if the judge had not been the upright Master Mei but one willing to listen to backers, he would very nearly have gone home empty-handed. So I record this to show merchants: at the very start, when your goods are about to be released for sale, look carefully at the broker across from you; only then can you let the goods go and be sure of no mishap.

stories.title_en: Alarming Words Goad a Man Back to Gambling

paragraphs.zh: 张士升，莒溪人，膏粱子弟也。父致万金，均分于士升兄弟，田园膏腴，坐享成业。一旦父卒，时初行万历钱，被棍徒引其赌博。彼富豪雏子，惟见场中饮酒豪放，可轻狂快意，哪知财帛当惜？不数月间，输去银数百两，尚欣欣喜赌，未肯休也。
paragraphs.en: Zhang Shisheng of Juxi was a pampered son of wealth. His father had amassed ten thousand taels and divided them equally among Shisheng and his brothers; the fields and gardens were fertile, and the sons lived at ease on a ready-made estate. When the father died, just as Wanli coins were first coming into circulation, swindlers lured Shisheng into gambling. A greenhorn from a rich house, he saw only the bold drinking and swagger of the gambling rooms—a wild and carefree life that suited him. How would he know that money is to be treasured? Within a few months he had lost several hundred taels of silver, yet he still went on gambling happily, with no thought of stopping.

paragraphs.zh: 乡有陈荣一者，乃士升父在日所用做中保供呼唤者。人虽微贱，却有忠义之心，不忍士升之被棍诱引也。乃备一盛筵，单请士升一人，酒筵中慢慢缓谈，将其父在日，始终生财缘由，爱惜钱米实事，一一从头细讲；且赞羡其能，慨叹其苦，后又谈及民情世故，及钱米难得之状，穷民无钱之苦，因劝之曰：“令先尊发此巨富非易，你须念先人勤劳，保守基业，切不可去赌。前者虽赌去数百金，已往勿咎；但从今改过，依旧坐享福泽矣。”士升见荣一词情恳切，一时良心发动，曰：“吾依你言，从今誓不赌也。”次日棍徒引之，果不去赌。众方怪异，后知出于荣一所劝，无可奈何，商议曰：“谁能引其再赌者，众敛十金与之。”有柴昆者曰：“我能引之。”众将银十两封存。
paragraphs.en: In the village lived a man named Chen Rongyi, whom Shisheng's late father had employed as a trusted household agent. Humble as he was, he possessed a loyal and upright heart and could not bear to watch Shisheng being led astray by swindlers. So he prepared a fine feast and invited Shisheng alone. Over wine, he spoke slowly and at length: from beginning to end, he recounted how the father had built his fortune and exactly how he had guarded every coin and every grain of rice. He praised the father's ability and sighed over his hardships; then he spoke of worldly ways, of how hard cash and rice are to come by, and of the misery of the poor who have none. At last he urged him: "It was not easy for your late father to amass such wealth. You must remember your forebears' toil and hold on to the family foundation. Whatever you do, stop gambling. True, you have already lost several hundred taels, but let bygones be bygones. Mend your ways from today, and you can still live at ease on the family fortune." Shisheng saw that Rongyi's words were earnest, and for a moment his conscience stirred. "I will do as you say," he said. "From today I swear off gambling." The next day the swindlers came for him, and sure enough he would not go. The gang was baffled; when they later learned it was Rongyi's doing, there was nothing they could do. They took counsel: "Whoever can get him gambling again, we will pool ten taels for him." A man named Chai Kun said, "I can do it." The gang sealed up ten taels of silver as the prize.

paragraphs.zh: 昆见士升在路亭闲坐，挨近其身，先闲谈他事，后问曰：“闻汝今收手不赌乎？”士升曰：“然。”昆曰：“赌非好事，今能自知回头，真是豪杰。盛族富家子弟，果有知识高人，我真羡服！只外人都传，是荣一老劝你而止。果是他劝否？”士升曰：“的是得他劝。”柴昆嗟叹曰：“荣一小辈奔走下贱之流，岂是你父兄，岂是你叔伯，何禁止得人？你名门子弟，聪明男子，何待贱人训诲？使路人传你听下贱人主使，皆暗中非笑，谓你无能为。依我所见，还当暂出小赌，过了半月一月，自己收手，人便说你是自不爱赌，非关听下辈命令也。如此方是大丈夫所为，不羞了故家门风。”士升是无识雏子，闻此佞言，心自猜曰：“果是我今若便止，人道是荣一之功。须再去赌一月，然后自止，岂不挺豪杰哉！”随即入场复赌。柴昆暗领众银而去。
paragraphs.en: Kun found Shisheng sitting idly in a roadside pavilion. He sidled up, chatted of this and that, and then asked, “Is it true you have quit gambling?” Shisheng said it was. Kun said, “Gambling is a bad business. To see that and turn back on your own—that is the mark of a true hero. For the son of a great and wealthy house to show such sense, I honestly admire you. Only—everyone is saying it was old Rongyi who talked you into stopping. Is that really so?” Shisheng said, “It is. It was his advice.” Chai Kun sighed. “Rongyi is a low-life crook, a mere runner of errands. Is he your father or brother? Is he your uncle? What right has he to forbid you anything? You are the son of a famous family, a clever man—why take instruction from a scoundrel? If word gets around that you take orders from a low fellow, people will laugh at you behind your back and say you have no spine. In my view, you should go back for a little light gambling. After half a month or a month, quit on your own. Then people will say you stopped because you no longer cared for gambling, not because you obeyed a servant's orders. That is how a true man acts, and it brings no shame on your family's name.” Shisheng was a witless greenhorn. Hearing this smooth, false talk, he thought to himself: “True enough—if I stop now, people will call it Rongyi's achievement. Better to gamble another month and then quit on my own. Won't I stand out as a hero then?” He went straight back to the gambling rooms. Chai Kun quietly collected the gang's silver and left.

paragraphs.zh: 士升赌了一月，野心复逞。后荣一虽言，亦不见纳，终至于尽赌倾家。皆柴昆一激之也，其祸烈也。
paragraphs.en: Shisheng gambled a month, and his wild heart broke out again. Later, though Rongyi spoke, he would not take it in, and in the end gambled until the house was emptied. All this was Chai Kun’s one goad; the disaster was fierce.

paragraphs.zh: 按：士升惑柴昆之瞽说，拒荣一之忠言，徒以其人卑微，谓受其谏为耻。不知尧请问下民，舜下询荛，周公走迎乎下士，韩信乞策于左车。彼帝王将相，犹俯听微言若是，岂以人之贱而可废其言之善乎！惜士升黄口之子，目不知古今，故中谗言而不察也。噫！
paragraphs.en: Note: Shisheng was confused by Chai Kun’s blind talk and rejected Rongyi’s loyal words, merely because the man was lowly, and thought it shameful to take his counsel. He did not know that Yao inquired of the common people, Shun asked down to the grass-cutters, the Duke of Zhou hurried out to meet lesser gentlemen, and Han Xin begged plans from Li Zuoche. Those emperors, kings, and generals still bent to hear humble words like that—can you discard a good word because the man is low? Pity that Shisheng was a yellow-mouthed boy who knew nothing of past and present, so he fell for slander and did not see it. Alas!

stories.title_en: Posing as a Young Lord, Using a Courtesan to Strip a Gambler

paragraphs.zh: 王荻溪，万金之子。好赌无厌，多被赌朋合谋，尽倾其家。后收拾餘资，只得三百两，乃带一仆，复往县中赌。众棍后合本，迭来与赌。时荻溪家已尽破，而赌已学得甚高，虽未能胜众棍，亦不至为棍所胜。相持半月余，无好子弟到，无雏家可网，乃投府去。更无大赌场可快意者，遂往嫖李细卿家。
paragraphs.en: Wang Dixi was the son of a family worth ten thousand taels. He loved gambling insatiably, and his gambling friends conspired against him so often that his whole fortune was lost. Later he scraped together what capital remained—barely three hundred taels—took a single servant, and went back to the county town to gamble. The sharps there pooled their funds and took turns at the table with him. By then Dixi's household was ruined, but his skill at gambling had grown very high: he could not beat the pack of sharps, yet they could not beat him either. For over half a month they held each other off, but no new young gentlemen came to town and there were no greenhorns to net. So Dixi went on to the prefectural city; and since no gambling den there was big enough to please him either, he went to visit the courtesan Li Xiqing.

paragraphs.zh: 有二三赌伙寻至府，闻荻溪已入妓家，众即划计曰：“如此如此笼络之，可尽夺其金矣。”次日，候荻溪出外寻赌伙，即入对细卿曰：“荻溪只好赌，不好嫖，彼无厚物与你。今依我如此如此行，先送你二十两人事。后赌得的，每一百两复许加二抽。”细卿许诺，午设盛馔，方与荻溪入席饮数杯。忽二家人来送礼物，辉煌熳烂，皆上好物件，约值二十餘金。曰：“公子命送此薄仪，少倾便到。”细卿逐一看过，尽数收起，以茶待二家人于外，复来席陪荻溪，且喜且作懊恼之意。荻溪曰：“是何人送你厚礼，你反似犹闷，何故？”细卿曰：“不问正难开口。此是黄公子送的。旧年在此赌钱，输去银千餘两，我亦得他厚惠。今日将到，望相公赦我，妾须出去迎他。容后日多陪相公几日，以补罪。”荻溪曰：“既是公子，我便出外让他。”细卿喜曰：“相公如此宽容，是妾有二天也。”荻溪将拂衣起，细卿挽住曰：“少坐不妨！更有一件，此人极活泼无崖岸。少间乘机提起，若请相见，或在此同话，为我陪客。得借重高贤，亦为我增声价也。”荻溪本欲避席，只闻公子旧在此赌，心中早已喜十分。使一仆伏侍，在内独酌，叫细卿出外迎客。
paragraphs.en: Two or three of his gambling partners tracked him down to the house. Hearing that Dixi had gone into the brothel, they hatched a plan: "We will rope him in this way, and we can take every coin he has." The next day, waiting until Dixi had gone out to find his gambling partners, they went inside and said to Xiqing: "Dixi only likes gambling, not women; he has no rich gifts for you. Do as we tell you: first, we will send you twenty taels as a gift; afterward, from whatever we win at the table, you shall get an extra two taels per hundred." Xiqing agreed. At noon she laid out a lavish meal, and she and Dixi had drunk only a few cups when two menservants suddenly arrived bearing gifts—dazzling, splendid things, all first-rate, worth more than twenty taels. "Our young lord sends this trifling token," they said. "He will be here shortly." Xiqing looked the gifts over one by one, had them all put away, served tea to the two servants outside, then returned to the table to keep Dixi company—half delighted, half putting on a show of vexation. Dixi said, "Someone sends you rich gifts, and you look put out instead. Why?" Xiqing said, "If you had not asked, I could hardly have brought it up. These are from Young Lord Huang. Last year he gambled here and lost more than a thousand taels, and he was generous to me besides. He is due to arrive today. I beg your pardon, sir—I must go out to welcome him. Let me make it up to you with extra days of company afterward." Dixi said, "If it is a young lord, I will step out and leave the field to him." Xiqing said brightly, "With such forbearance, sir, you are a second heaven to me." Dixi made to rise, but she held him back. "Sit a while longer, it does no harm. One thing more: this man is lively and without pretensions. In a while, if the chance arises and he asks to meet you, or wants to talk here together, keep him company for me. If you lend me your worthy presence, it raises my standing too." Dixi had meant to leave the table, but the moment he heard that the young lord used to gamble here, his heart was already ten parts pleased. He kept his one servant to wait on him, drank alone in the inner room, and sent Xiqing out to receive the guest.

paragraphs.zh: 须臾，公子到，细卿从容奉茶。叙寒温讫，公子径起，欲入内游玩。细卿慌忙请止，曰：“适有一外亲远来，在内留一水饭，恐无处可避也。”公子笑曰：“孤老便是孤老，何须托外亲也？既是你情人，我生平不吃醋，便请相见何妨？”即遣二仆入请。尚未出，又促细卿曰：“汝去请之。”细卿入内邀出。公子张看荻溪一表非俗，呵呵笑曰：“细卿妙人，果会择好才子。”即降前叙礼，院内备筵已到，公子坐上，荻溪前，细卿左陪。席间谈笑，并不及赌中去。到晚，索骰子行令，公子耍曰：“只恐卑人未晓好色。”细卿曰：“公子有一掷百万之豪，荻卿亦有呼庐赐绯之兴，愧小婢未足当好色耳。”公子曰：“荻溪亦作家乎？明早略赌一东道何如？”荻溪曰：“东道当小弟奉，何劳赌也？”公子曰：“空食未佳，须赢为奇。”先取掷之，无色。荻溪一掷即胜。公子须再加一台戏，又输；热性一起，曰：“荻溪有此妙手乎！与汝再决输赢。”荻溪曰：“不敢扳高耳，亦愿陪。”两下赌起，互有胜负。
paragraphs.en: Presently the young lord arrived, and Xiqing served tea with an easy grace. When the usual civilities were done, the young lord got straight up, meaning to stroll into the inner rooms. Xiqing hurriedly begged him to stop. “A kinsman from elsewhere has just come a long way,” she said, “and is inside having a simple meal. I am afraid there is nowhere for him to withdraw.” The young lord laughed. “A lover is a lover—why dress him up as an outside kinsman? If he is your man, I have never been the jealous sort. What harm is there in asking him out to meet me?” He sent two servants in to invite him. When they did not come out at once, he pressed Xiqing: “You go and ask him.” Xiqing went in and brought Di Xi out. The young lord looked him over—a fine figure, no common man—and laughed, “Xiqing is a woman of taste; she really does know how to pick a fine gentleman.” He came forward and they exchanged courtesies. The banquet ordered for the courtyard had arrived; the young lord took the seat of honor, Di Xi sat facing him, and Xiqing sat at the left in attendance. All through the meal they talked and laughed, never once touching on gambling. At nightfall they called for dice to play drinking games. The young lord joked, “I only fear I don't yet know a true connoisseur of beauty when I see one.” Xiqing said, “The young lord has the dash to stake a million on a single cast, and Di Xi has the zest to shout for the winning throw and claim the prize. This poor girl is only ashamed she is no great beauty to be fond of.” The young lord said, “So Di Xi is a real player too? Tomorrow morning, what say we gamble for a small treat?” Di Xi said, “The treat is mine to offer—no need to gamble for it.” The young lord said, “A meal that costs nothing has no savor; it must be won to be worth anything.” He took the dice and threw first—nothing. Di Xi won with a single cast. The young lord raised the stake by another play and lost again. His blood was up. “Di Xi, what a hand you have! Once more, you and I, to settle win and loss.” Di Xi said, “I would not presume to reach so high, but I am game to keep you company.” The two fell to gambling, and the wins went back and forth.

paragraphs.zh: 至一更，公子输上百金。细卿亦抽头十餘两矣，即将骰子收起，曰：“今日乘轿劳顿，夜已深矣，须去睡。明日看戏时酒席中再翻，稍抬举我抽头。”公子以输多，发怒要赌。荻溪亦发大言曰：“若再来，须百金一堆，不然且罢！”公子先取定银在，以一百为堆。细卿故执骰不与。公子大怒曰：“只凭一掷，随有无便罢！”细卿付还骰。公子一掷即胜，得百金，曰：“更照前一堆。”又胜；曰：“我生平好大不好细，须二百为堆。”方发性间，忽闻门外火把轿来。慌入报曰：“老爷跟寻至急，可速回去！”公子曰：“我色方来，奈何阻我兴！”其后一掷，又赢二百为堆。家人催如星火，公子曰：“我明日昼间不来，夜定来矣。”荻溪留之，不能得。细卿亦惊作痴呆样，慌忙送别。归怨荻溪曰：“人无全胜。你先赢许多，须当知止。奈何公子欲翻，你更出大堆，是不晓避色也。空作惯家，不及我妇人见矣。”荻溪曰：“吾万金赌尽，何数他三百两！有甚大事，空怨恨为！”在细卿家留宿数日；再留之，坚辞而去。
paragraphs.en: By the first watch, the young lord had lost over a hundred taels, and Xiqing had already taken her cut of ten-plus taels. She gathered up the dice and said, "You have had a tiring day in the sedan chair, and the night is deep; you must go to sleep. Tomorrow, over wine at the play, we can settle the score, and perhaps show me a little favor with the cut." The young lord, having lost heavily, flew into a temper and demanded to continue. Di Xi too made a bold declaration: "If we go on, it must be a hundred taels a pile, or we stop!" The young lord produced ready silver and stacked it a hundred to the pile. Xiqing deliberately held onto the dice and refused to hand them over. The young lord flared up: "One throw only—win or lose, we are done!" Xiqing returned the dice. The young lord won on a single cast and took the hundred taels. "Another pile, same as before," he said. He won again. "All my life I have liked big stakes, never small ones. Make it two hundred a pile." Just as he was working himself into a fever, torches and a sedan chair were suddenly heard at the gate. A servant rushed in: "His Lordship is searching for you urgently; you must return at once!" The young lord said, "My luck has just turned—why spoil my run?" His next throw won another two-hundred pile. The servants pressed him as if the house were on fire. "Tomorrow I cannot come by day," the young lord said, "but at night I will surely be here." Di Xi tried to keep him, without success. Xiqing put on a stunned, witless look of fright and hurried to see him off. Then she came back and rounded on Di Xi: "No one wins forever. You had won a great deal at first; you should have known when to stop. When the young lord wanted to win it back, why did you put out even bigger piles? That is not knowing how to avoid a winning streak. A fine old hand you are—your judgment does not match a mere woman's." Di Xi said, "I have gambled away ten thousand taels in my time. What is a mere three hundred to me? What is the great matter, that you should fret and fume over it?" He stayed on at Xiqing's house for several days; when she pressed him to stay longer, he firmly declined and left.

paragraphs.zh: 按：公子是装来的，先以厚礼送妓，令荻溪信为真公子。后来圈套，皆是装成。其药骰已先藏在细卿手，故令其抢起真骰，然后以药骰付还之，使其不疑。三执皆胜，套定催归，其谁防之？然荻溪虽作家，安能测其弊哉！吁！凡赌博者，弊外生弊，鉴此而知机，收手勿赌，真良策也，莫如彼之一旦尽囊而空矣！
paragraphs.en: Note: The young lord was an impostor. He first sent lavish gifts to the courtesan to make Dixi believe he was a real nobleman; everything thereafter was staged. The loaded dice had already been hidden in Xiqing's hand, which is why she snatched up the honest dice and then handed back the loaded ones, so he would suspect nothing. Three throws, three wins; once the trap was set to urge him home, who could guard against it? Yet even Dixi, a practiced hand, could not have fathomed such a cheat. In gambling, tricks breed beyond tricks. To see the snare in this story, recognize the moment, and take your hand off the table for good—that is the truly sound plan. Do not end like him, with your whole purse emptied in a single day.

stories.title_en: A Lover of Gambling Falls into Someone Else’s Trick

paragraphs.zh: 闽人徐华胜，号含秀。为人矜夸骄亢，酷好赌钱。一日，买纸往京卖。有张鄂号叔真者，先富，因赌倾折，后有餘囊数百两，亦买纸往京卖。二人同县异乡，托处共店。鄂心怀一术，每在店中与华胜着棋，或赌东道，或赌时果。鄂棋本能让华胜一车，鄂乃孤客，徐姓众多，鄂每诈输东道，暗结华之乡亲，使钳其口，无得而议论之。故输五而赢二，而华胜不知鄂怀锋而之。
paragraphs.en: Xu Huasheng of Fujian, styled Hanxiu, was boastful and arrogant by nature, and he loved gambling fiercely. One day, he bought a stock of paper to sell in the capital. There was also a man named Zhang E, styled Shuzhen, who had once been rich but was ruined by gambling; he still had a few hundred taels left in his purse and had also bought paper to sell in the capital. The two were from the same county but different hometowns, lodging at the same inn. E had a scheme in mind. He often played chess with Huasheng at the inn, sometimes betting on a treat, sometimes on seasonal fruit. In truth, E's chess was strong enough to give Huasheng a chariot, but E was a lone traveler while the Xu clan was numerous. So E often lost the treat on purpose, while secretly winning over Huasheng's fellow townsmen, silencing them so they would say nothing about it. He would lose five games and win only two, yet Huasheng never guessed that E was hiding his true sharpness.

paragraphs.zh: 一日，鄂已睡，华胜邀起而赌东道。鄂心喜曰：“此夜机会可矣。”故推不起。又强之，鄂曰：“我不赌东道，要赌银。”胜心暗忖：“我棋高他，何惧之有？”连声应曰：“更好。”不知已堕其术矣。且素性亢傲，乡亲咸憎之，大家赞成其赌。鄂曰：“先以银对定，输即收去，无得抵赖。要一两一局，每两与众抽头二钱，作东道并做戏。”胜曰：“虽二两无妨。”未几，输数局。心中热起，说要十两一局。客中老成者曰：“不可，且休矣！”其后生辈反以言激之。胜心益热，再对银十两而赌。不数局，共输数十餘两。时天色已曙，鄂将胜银卷入囊中而起。胜邀再赌，鄂坚执不许，二人相扭甚热。鄂曰：“是你邀我赌，非我邀你赌。我若输你，肯饶否？我家财数千，因赌而倾。你输此些小，何得鼻血？好不为男子也！任你经官不还。”客中老成者曰：“是我辈无见识，不阻你，以致覆败。但张兄说得是，倘他输你，必不放他。不如我辈抽头者尽还你罢。俗云‘豪杰对豪杰，齿打落，吞肚里’。”鄂曰：“众既以抽头者退出，我亦退银三两做戏，更出一两作东道。内抽五钱，换金一线，打一戒指与徐兄，作好赌之戒。”众曰：“张兄之言大有理，乃豪杰惜豪杰，真慷慨丈夫也！”华胜默然。真个是：“安分不贪难诱引，贪心萌内必遭殃。”
paragraphs.en: One evening, Zhang E was already asleep when Huasheng roused him to gamble for a treat. E was delighted: "Tonight is the chance." So he feigned reluctance and refused to get up. When pressed again, E said, "I will not gamble for a treat; we must gamble for silver." Sheng thought to himself, "My chess skills are superior; what do I have to fear?" He answered at once, "Even better." Unaware that he had fallen into their trap, he proceeded. Moreover, being naturally arrogant and detested by his fellow townspeople, everyone egged the wager on. E said, "First, let us weigh out the silver face to face; the loser pays immediately, no backing out. One tael per game, with two qian from each tael going to the company as a cut to cover the treat and the show." Sheng said, "Two taels is no problem." Before long, he lost several games. His blood heated, and he demanded ten taels per game. The older, steadier guests said, "No—you should stop now." The younger ones provoked him further. Sheng's blood grew hotter; he weighed out another ten taels and played on. Within a few more games, he had lost dozens of taels in total. By then, dawn was breaking. E swept the winnings into his bag and stood up. Sheng begged him to play on; E flatly refused, and the two grappled fiercely. E said, "You invited me to gamble, not I you. If I had lost to you, would you have let me off? My family had several thousand taels, and gambling emptied it. You have lost this trifling sum—why the fuss? Are you really a man? Take me to the magistrate if you like; I will not pay it back." The older guests said, "It was we who lacked the sense to stop you, leading to your ruin. But Brother Zhang is right: if he had lost to you, you would never have let him go. Better that those of us who took the cut return it all to you. As the saying goes: when hero meets hero, a knocked-out tooth is swallowed and done with." E said, "Since the company is returning the cut, I too will give back three taels for the show and add one tael more for the treat. From it, take five qian, exchange it for a thread of gold, and have a ring made for Brother Xu as a warning against gambling—for 'ring' and 'warning' share the same character." The company all said, "Brother Zhang's words are most reasonable. This is a hero cherishing a hero, a truly generous man." Huasheng fell silent. Truly it is said: keep to your lot and covet nothing, and no one can lure you; let greed sprout within, and ruin is sure to follow.

paragraphs.zh: 按：好赌者落人圈套，何止若是。鄂犹是有本富商，故不尽取，而又善处于终，致戒其后。若赌场中光棍，何怕你万贯家财，尽落于伊手乎！睹徐华胜之输而返悔者，后人鉴之，可勿蹈矣。
paragraphs.en: Note: Gamblers falling into snares suffer far worse fates than this. E, being a wealthy merchant with capital, was not cleaned out entirely; he handled the conclusion skillfully, leaving a warning for others. Had it been a sharp con man in a gambling den, what care would he have for your ten-thousand-tael fortune? Every last coin would have fallen into his hands. Let those who come after look at Xu Huasheng, who lost everything and repented too late—take warning and do not tread the same path.

stories.title_en: Posing as a Young Lord to Swindle a Merchant’s Silver

paragraphs.zh: 陈栋，山东人也，屡年入福建建阳地名长埂贩买机布。万历三十二年季春，同二仆带银壹千馀两，复往长埂买布。途逢一棍，窥其银多，欲谋之。见栋乃老练惯客，每迟行早宿，关防严密，难以动手。诈称福建分巡建南道公子，甚有规模态度，乃带四仆，一路与栋同店。棍不与栋交语，而栋亦不之顾也。
paragraphs.en: Chen Dong was a man of Shandong. For years he went to Changgeng in Jianyang, Fujian, to buy loom cloth. In the third month of Wanli 32, with two servants and over a thousand taels of silver, he again went to Changgeng to buy cloth. On the way he met a ruffian who spied that he had much silver and wanted to scheme for it. Seeing Dong was a seasoned old traveler, always starting late and lodging early, with tight precautions, it was hard to make a move. He pretended to be the son of the Fujian Circuit Intendant of Jiannan Circuit, with quite the air and manner, and brought four servants, lodging at the same inns as Dong all the way. The ruffian did not speak with Dong, and Dong paid him no attention.

paragraphs.zh: 直至江西铅山县，其县丞姓蔡名渊者，乃广东人也，与巡道同府异县，素不相识。棍往拜之。县丞闻是巡道公子，待之甚厚，即来回拜，送下程。栋见县丞回拜，信其为真公子。是夜，棍以下程请栋。栋欢领之，而心中犹谨防他盗，不敢痛饮；棍犹动手不得。次日，经乌石宿。其地非大口岸，栋欲办酒回礼，以无物可买而止。
paragraphs.en: They traveled on until they reached Yanshan county in Jiangxi. The assistant magistrate there, Cai Yuan by name, was a Cantonese—from the same prefecture as the circuit intendant but a different county—and the two had never met. The con man went to call on him. Hearing that this was the circuit intendant’s son, the assistant magistrate treated him handsomely, then came in person to return the call and sent provisions for the road. When Dong saw the assistant magistrate return the visit, he believed the man was a legitimate heir. That night the con man invited Dong to share the gift. Dong accepted gladly, but inwardly he still kept careful guard against theft and dared not drink deep, so the con man still found no chance to strike. The next day they stopped for the night at Wushi. It was no major port; Dong wanted to lay on a return feast, but with nothing there to buy, he let the idea drop.

paragraphs.zh: 又次日，到崇安县宿。栋心谓：此到长埂旧主不远，犹其外之故家也。且来日与公子别矣，不答敬殊非礼也，遂买肴馔请之。棍谓栋曰：“同舟过江，前缘非偶。与君一路同来，岂非偶乎？明日与君分路，燕鸿南北，未知何日再会，各开怀畅饮。”延至三更，其仆皆困顿熟睡。栋醉甚，亦伏桌睡。棍遂将栋之财物悉偷去。
paragraphs.en: The day after that they lodged in Chong'an county. Dong thought to himself: From here it is not far to my old host at Changgeng—he is like family away from home. And tomorrow I part from the young lord; not to return his hospitality would be poor manners. So he bought meat and wine and invited the man to dinner. The con man said to Dong: "To cross a river in the same boat is a bond from a former life, not mere chance. You and I have come the whole way together—how is that not fate? Tomorrow we take separate roads, like the swallow and the wild goose, one flying south, one north, and who knows when we shall meet again. Let us each open our hearts and drink deep." They spun the drinking out to the third watch. The servants were all worn out and fast asleep. Dong, very drunk, also fell asleep slumped over the table. The con man then sneaked off with every bit of Dong's money and goods.

paragraphs.zh: 待栋醒觉，不知棍何处去矣。即在崇安县告店家通同作弊。随即往江西广信府，告其县丞勾引光棍，而以原店家作证。县丞诉曰：“福建巡道实与我同府异县，其人姓氏，我素知之；但公子并未会面，他称其姓氏来拜我，我乃县丞小官，安得不回他拜，不送他赆？今至崇安已经数日，盗你银去，与我何干？”栋曰：“那棍一路同来，我防之甚切。他来谒你，而你回拜，我方信是真公子，故堕其术。今其人系你相识，安得不告你？”本府不能判断。栋又在史大巡处告。史爷判是县丞不合错拜公子，轻易便送下程，致误客商，不无公错。谅断银壹百两，与栋作盘缠之资而归。
paragraphs.en: When Dong awoke, the con man was nowhere to be found. He promptly filed a complaint in Chong'an county accusing the innkeeper of colluding in the swindle, then went on to Guangxin Prefecture in Jiangxi and charged the assistant magistrate with being in league with the sharp, naming the innkeeper as his witness. The assistant magistrate protested: "The Fujian circuit intendant really is from my prefecture, though a different county, and I have long known his name. But I had never met his son. He came to call on me under that name, and I am a mere assistant magistrate—how could I not return his call or send him a parting gift? By the time you reached Chong'an, days had passed. He stole your silver—what has that to do with me?" Dong said: "That crook traveled with me the whole way, and I guarded against him closely. Only when he called on you and you returned the call did I believe he was a true young lord, and so I fell into his trap. Since the man is an acquaintance of yours, how can I not bring the charge against you?" The prefecture could not decide the case. Dong then brought it before Inspector Shi. Master Shi ruled that the assistant magistrate had improperly returned the call to a false "young lord" and sent provisions too readily, thereby misleading a traveling merchant—it was not without official negligence. He saw fit to award Dong one hundred taels of silver as travel money for the journey home.

paragraphs.zh: 噫：棍之设机巧矣！一路妆作公子，商人犹知防之。至拜县丞，而县丞回拜送赆，孰不以为真公子也？又先设机以请商人，则商人备礼以答敬，亦理所必然也。乃故缠饮，困其主仆，则乘夜行窃易矣。故曰其设机最巧也。使栋更能慎防一夜，则棍奸无所施。故慎始不如慎终，日乾更继以夕惕，斯可万无一失。不然，抱瓮汲井，几至井口而败其瓮，与不慎何异？吾愿为商者，处终如谨始可也。
paragraphs.en: Note: Ah, how cleverly this swindler laid his trap! All along the road he played the young lord, and the merchant still knew to be on guard. But once he called on the assistant magistrate, and the magistrate returned the call and sent a gift, who would not have taken him for a genuine young lord? And since the trap had been laid by playing host first, the merchant’s return of the courtesy was only natural. Then he deliberately dragged out the drinking to wear down master and servants, and stealing in the night was easy. That is why I call his trap the cleverest kind. Had he kept his guard up just one more night, the swindler’s scheme would have had nowhere to bite. So vigilance at the start counts for less than vigilance at the end: diligent by day and watchful by night—only then is there absolutely no room for error. Otherwise it is like hauling a jar of water up from a well and smashing it just as it reaches the well’s mouth—how is that different from never being careful at all? My wish for merchants is this: be as careful at the end as you were at the beginning.

stories.title_en: Showing Off Clothes and Dress Wakes a Thief’s Heart

paragraphs.zh: 游天生，徽州府人。丰采俊雅，好装饰。尝同一仆徐丁携本银五百馀两，往建宁府买铁。始到崇安县，搭一青流船，艄公名李雅，水手名翁迓。雅先以嫖赌破家，后无赖而撑船。其时船至建阳县，天生起岸，往拜乡亲。将衣箱打开，取出衣服鲜丽，所带用物俱美。雅一见生心。
paragraphs.en: You Tiansheng was from Huizhou Prefecture—handsome and elegant in bearing, fond of fine dress. Once, accompanied by a single servant, Xu Ding, and carrying over five hundred taels of capital, he set out for Jianning Prefecture to buy iron. Upon reaching Chong'an County, he boarded a Qingliu-type boat. The boatman was named Li Ya, the deckhand Weng Ya. Ya had previously ruined his family through whoring and gambling; left penniless, he took to poling boats. When the vessel arrived at Jianyang County, Tiansheng went ashore to visit fellow townspeople. He opened his clothes chest, revealing bright, handsome garments; everything he carried was of excellent quality. The moment Ya caught sight of it, greed seized him.

paragraphs.zh: 至晚，天生叫艄公买些酒馔。雅暗将陀陀花入酒中———陀陀花者，乃三年茄花也，人服此则昏迷不能语。是夜，天生主仆中了此毒，醉不能醒。三鼓时候，雅邀水手行谋。水手曰：“钱财有命，不可逆理妄求。倘若事泄，罪将安逃？吾不敢为也。”雅狠心一起，不听水手之阻，将其主仆推入深潭。天生淹死，徐丁幸饮酒少，入水复苏，颇识水性，水上岸。次日，搭后船往建宁府，即抱牌告于王大爷。当差捕兵六名，同徐丁到临江门去缉拿。临江门，乃建宁往来诸船凑集之口岸也。是时李雅谋财在手，正买酒上船，思量作乐。徐丁认得，即引捕兵擒锁，搜其赃物，尚在船中。遂并入赃，俱拿到府。
paragraphs.en: That evening Tiansheng told the boatman to buy some wine and food. Ya secretly slipped tuotuo blossoms into the wine—the tuotuo is the flower of a three-year eggplant, and whoever takes it falls senseless and cannot speak. That night Tiansheng and his servant took the poison and sank into a stupor from which they could not wake. At the third drum, Ya invited the deckhand to join the plot. The deckhand said: "Wealth is allotted by fate; you cannot chase it against all right. If this gets out, where will you flee from the crime? I will have no part in it." But a ruthless resolve rose in Ya; he ignored the deckhand's protest and pushed master and servant into a deep pool. Tiansheng drowned. Xu Ding, luckily, had drunk little; he came to in the water and, being familiar with the water, made it up the bank. The next day he caught a later boat to Jianning Prefecture and lodged a formal complaint before Master Wang. Six constables were assigned to go with Xu Ding to the Linjiang Gate wharf to make the arrest—Linjiang Gate being the port where all boats to and from Jianning gathered. Just then Li Ya, the stolen money in hand, was buying wine to take aboard, planning to make merry. Xu Ding recognized him and led the constables to seize and chain him; a search turned up the loot, still on the boat. They took him, loot and all, to the prefecture.

paragraphs.zh: 王爷审问。雅见事露，难以推托，一概供招，攀及水手同谋。徐丁曰：“我当中毒时，酩酊不能言，如梦中，闻得水手劝阻，不与同谋，已先逃去。今若枉及此人，令后人不肯向善也。”王爷即将李雅责四十板收监，依律拟斩。其行李并原银，差防夫二名，同徐丁直解至天生家去。李雅次年冬季处决。后水手翁迓弃船归农，颇致丰足。雅以谋人而促死，迓以阻谏而全家，谚曰：“善有善报，恶有恶报”，信不虚也。
paragraphs.en: Prince Wang held the hearing. Seeing the affair was out and denial useless, Ya confessed to everything—and dragged in the deckhand as an accomplice. Xu Ding said: “When I was poisoned I was dead drunk and could not speak, as if in a dream; but I heard the deckhand argue against it and refuse to join, and he had already fled. If we wrong this man now, it will make others unwilling to choose the good.” Prince Wang had Li Ya beaten forty strokes and thrown in jail, and sentenced him to beheading under the law. The baggage and the original silver were sent under two guards, together with Xu Ding, straight to Tiansheng’s family. Li Ya was executed in the winter of the following year. The deckhand Weng Ya later gave up the boat and went back to farming, and came to live in fair comfort. Li Ya plotted against others and hastened his own death; Weng Ya spoke against it and kept his family whole. As the proverb says, “Good is repaid with good, evil with evil”—truly, it is no empty saying.

paragraphs.zh: 按：游天生之召祸，良由衣服华丽，致使贼艄垂涎。大凡孤客搭船，切须提防贼艄谋害。昼宜略睡，夜方易醒。煮菜暖酒，尤防放毒。服宜朴素，勿太炫耀。故老子曰：“良贾深藏若虚。”孔子曰：“以约失之者鲜。”此诚养德之言，抑亦远祸之道也。
paragraphs.en: Note: The disaster You Tiansheng brought on himself truly came from his gorgeous clothes, which made the thief-boatman drool. In general, a lone traveler taking a boat must carefully guard against a thief-boatman’s harm. By day one should sleep a little, so that by night one wakes easily. When they cook vegetables and warm wine, be especially wary of poison. Clothes should be plain; do not show off too much. So Laozi said: “A good merchant hides his goods as if he had nothing.” Confucius said: “Those who fail by being sparing are few.” These are truly words for cultivating virtue, and also a way to keep disaster far.
